articles.title: How to hit better bunker shots: A complete guide to mastering the sand
articles.summary: In the first episode of Top 100 Sessions, David Armitage gives a masterclass on how to become a better bunker player.
articles.body:
There are few people in golf who know the bunker game better than David Armitage. He coaches all aspects of the game, but the sand is his specialty.

"I am the only guy that is dumb enough to write 144 pages about how to get out of bunkers," he says.

For most golfers, bunkers are a source of anxiety — a place to be avoided at all costs. For Armitage, the bunker is his happy place. And he wants it to be the same for his students.

That mission has led Armitage to dedicate himself to helping golfers of all skill levels understand the secrets to better bunker play. He has shared his expertise in his book, The Bunker Game: How to Play with Confidence from the Sand , and now in our latest Top 100 Teacher Sessions video, where he breaks down the techniques and adjustments that can turn any golfer into a more confident player from the sand.

Watch the video below or read on for a complete guide to mastering bunker play, courtesy of the man who — quite literally — wrote the book on it.

Just about every average recreational golfer is fearful of the sand. When they see a sand trap, they do everything they can to avoid them, because when they find one, it can lead to a big score.

"I think it all leads back to bad concepts [and] bad understanding of how to play the bunker shot," Armitage says.

The "standard" technique for bunker play has long been to severely open your stance, open your clubface and then swing down your feet line. However, that technique doesn't work for a majority of players. With that setup and strike, it requires tons of strength and clubhead speed to get the ball up on the green.

Another issue with this setup is that it makes it incredibly difficult to get the ball heading in the correct direction. With such an open setup, aim becomes quite difficult.

"It's going to be unpredictable how the ball is going to start," Armitage says. "Because I've got the face wide open, my feet left … I'm not going to be as predictable with my start line."

Chapter 2: Seve Ballesteros' influence on modern bunker play

For Armitage, the turning point in his bunker education came from one of golf's greatest short-game artists: Seve Ballesteros.

Armitage spent most of the beginning of his golf life in St. Andrews, where the bunkers are small and difficult to escape. And although he had taken lessons from many coaches, he still struggled with his play from the sand.

"I obviously was a strong young kid and could generate a lot of speed," Armitage says. "But I found it difficult to start the ball online. I found it difficult to generate distance."

That changed when he spent time with Ballesteros, who was near the end of his career and visited St. Andrews for corporate outings from time to time. During those visits, Armitage got to watch him hit bunker shots and picked up on some of his techniques, such as the simplicity of the setup.

"He hit all the shots from a square stance," Armitage says.

Armitage remembers watching Ballesteros demonstrate the shots and heading straight to a bunker to try them himself. The difference was immediate.

"I couldn't believe how it changed my bunker game and how the start lines became better straight away, how my distance control became better, and how it felt just easier," he says.

Armitage's approach to bunker play begins with nailing the setup. Rather than trying to create a complicated swing, he wants golfers to establish a position that makes the correct motion easier to produce.

"I'm looking at really square stance," he says. "I've opened the face. I'm then taking my grip, and then I have a wide stance, low handle, moving my chin, my sternum, and my belt buckle onto the ball or just in front of the ball."

The first key is getting into a wide stance. Armitage wants it wider than a golfer's driver stance, which helps lower the body and the handle. That, in turn, helps the ball get up.

He also recommends digging the feet into the sand slightly. This helps golfers feel the sand beneath them and understand what kind of lie they are dealing with. But consistency is important. Armitage doesn't want golfers digging in by a different amount every time they enter a bunker.

"You've gotta be consistent with your approach to that setup," he says.

The next key is moving the body forward. Armitage wants the chin, sternum and belt buckle to shift toward the target. He sees too many golfers moving their lower body forward while leaving the upper body behind, which moves the low point backward.

Instead, the sternum should be forward, with a little more flex in the lead knee. Armitage says this was something he always noticed in Ballesteros' setup.

For a standard greenside bunker shot, Armitage places the ball just in front of the middle of his stance. The strike point is in the middle, and the sternum is directly above or slightly in front of the ball. That position controls the low point of the swing.

"The club's gonna enter on the sand, on the line. It gets to its lower point, lowest point where my sternum is, and then it exits out," he says.

Once the setup is in place, Armitage turns his attention to the clubface. The face still needs to be open, but the reason is different from the traditional approach. He wants an open face so golfers can expose the bounce of the wedge, which helps the club glide through the sand instead of digging into it.

"This is a beautiful part of the club that Gene Sarazen developed," Armitage says.

The bounce is the part of the sole that helps the club move through the sand. Opening the face exposes more of it, allowing the club to slide rather than dig.

Armitage also points out that golfers need to use the right club for the sand they are playing from. Different bunkers have different types of sand, and different wedges have different amounts of bounce.

"If you have a lot of bounce and you have a hard sand, that's probably not a great combination," he says.

For his standard greenside bunker shot, Armitage opens the face to about 2 o'clock. He uses a clock-face reference to explain the position: 12 o'clock is square, 1 o'clock is slightly open, and 2 o'clock is more open. (Left-handed golfers would use the opposite side of the clock, with 11 o'clock being slightly open, and 10 o'clock being more open.)

Armitage also recommends taking the grip after opening the face, which helps keep the face open through the shot.

He sometimes uses a slightly weaker left-hand grip, which helps prevent the face from closing too much. It's not something every golfer has to do, but it's a technique that can be useful and that is used by many tour players.

Armitage's standard bunker shot is 12-yards, which is what another short-game guru, Phil Mickelson, uses as his starting point. All other shots work from that standard 12-yard shot.

For the standard shot, the setup remains the same as described above. Then, the club needs to swing up and down into the sand.

"A lot of people talk about, like, do I pick the club up? Well, I think the club does have to go up," Armitage says. "Because we do need a steeper angle of attack in the bunker."

The key is that the setup should make this happen naturally. With the weight forward and the sternum in front of the ball, the club should swing more vertically without the golfer having to force it.

As you approach impact, Armitage wants the clubhead to enter the sand about two inches behind the ball and create a divot pattern that moves slightly left of the target line.If you can do that, the ball should pop nicely out of the sand.

As you make your swing, be sure you keep the weight forward throughout the motion. If you start with 70 to 75 percent of your weight on your lead foot, you wants that pressure to remain there through the backswing and increase into impact. The other important ingredient is speed. The sand slows the club down, so golfers need enough speed to get the ball out.

"Most amateurs, if they hit that shot, they're out of trouble, they've got a putter in their hand, and they're probably gonna make bogey and move on to the next hole with a smile."

Once golfers understand the basic bunker shot, you need to learn how to change distance without changing the swing speed. For that, Armitage suggests using different wedges and different face positions.

He has a gap wedge, a 54-degree wedge and a 60-degree wedge. With each club, he can use a square face, a 1 o'clock face, or a 2 o'clock face. That gives him nine different shots without changing the swing speed.

The type of sand, how much sand is taken, and how the club deflects through it can all affect the trajectory. Armitage points out that tour players don't always create spin themselves. Sometimes the sand is responsible for the way the ball reacts.

"When they see a ball spinning, they think that the player's making it spin, and sometimes it's to do with the circumstances," he says.

For everyday golfers, the lesson is to focus on the setup and the strike rather than trying to manufacture spin.

Armitage's advanced bunker shot is designed for experienced golfers who need to hit a short-sided shot or get the ball to stop quickly.

"This is a shot that I wouldn't teach the everyday golfer," he says.

The shot begins by opening the face even more. Armitage moves from his normal 2 o'clock position to about 2:30, pushing the limits of how much loft he can create. The more open the face becomes, the more bounce is exposed. But it also means there is less of the clubface available to hit the ball with, making the margin for error even thinner.

For this shot, Armitage also weakens his left-hand grip, lowers the handle and widens his stance even more. Then, he makes the same swing he does for any other bunker shot. The result is a shot that launches higher and travels shorter. That allows him to swing with speed while keeping the ball from going too far.

"You can still have speed, and that ball's gonna go higher and shorter," he says.

For short-sided bunker shots, that speed is especially important. Armitage says golfers often become tentative when they are close to the hole, and that can lead to deceleration and leaving the ball in the bunker.

But Armitage also emphasizes that some bunker shots are simply not accessible. Even the best players in the world sometimes have to accept a difficult pin and give themselves a longer putt.

"Some shots are just not accessible," he says. "You've gotta take your punishment sometimes."

Armitage's practice philosophy is simple: start with the strike, not the ball.

One of his favorite drills uses a rake. He places it behind the ball so that if he sways or falls back during the swing, he will hit it. The drill helps golfers understand how vertical the swing needs to be for a proper bunker shot.

"If I drift off the ball on the backswing, I'm gonna hit the rake," Armitage says.

The rake also helps golfers make sure the downswing is vertical and forward. Armitage recommends starting slowly and using the drill to build the feeling of the correct motion.

"Do it slowly," he says. "Maybe just do it in very slow motion just to get the image and the feeling."

Another drill comes from Ernie Els. Armitage says Els would draw two lines in the sand, set up wide, and make swings that focused on contacting the sand between those lines. He would then make two or three of those swings before hitting a ball.

"That's what the pros do, and one of the best players in the world," Armitage says.

The lesson for amateurs is to do the same. Rather than immediately hitting balls, start by practicing the setup and the strike.

"Do the line drills first, get that impact where you want it, and then take that to the ball," he says.

"This provides a longer planning window, allowing you to spread costs over time and take advantage of monthly payment plans," Tennessee Athletics wrote.

articles.title: Teammates sounding as if Nick Emmanwori won’t play. Seahawks’ options for opener
articles.summary: The hyrbid safety/linebacker key to coach Mike Macdonald’s multiple defenses is still limited following arthroscopic ankle surgery in July.
articles.body:
Signs are the key piece the Seahawks defense uses to check-mate offenses may not be on the board week one.

Nick Emmanwori was a limited participant in practice Sunday. The Seahawks issued their first participation and injury report of the season, three days before Seattle hosts the New England Patriots Wednesday in the NFL kickoff game at Lumen Field.

Coach Mike Macdonald's hybrid safety/linebacker who tilts schemes and plays in the Super Bowl champions' favor has yet to practice fully since his arthroscopic ankle surgery in mid-July.

For the third consecutive practice Emmanwori was stretching with teammates and participating with them in warmups. Sunday, he and the Seahawks were in shells for the practice.

Macdonald and his defense featured Emmanwori almost everywhere on the field last season. They allowed the fewest points in the league, then dominated the Patriots in Super Bowl 60 in February.

Ernest Jones made it sound as if Emmanwori isn't going to be playing in the 2026 opener.

The middle linebacker and signal-caller knows what Emmanwori enables the Seahawks defense to do — and what it would be missing would be missing without him.

Emmanwori sprained the ankle he eventually got repaired in practice four days before the Super Bowl against the Patriots in February, yet played the entire game.

"We can do multiple things. We can put him in certain positions to dictate certain reps and how you want certain things to go," Jones said Sunday.

"He's definitely a big part of our defense. And when we get him back — we can't wait to get him back — but for right now we're focused on who's out there, who's available right now.

"And we know that when his time comes," Jones said with a chuckle of Emmanwori, "he's an alien. He can do whatever."

The Seahawks are working through alternatives for playing Wednesday without Emmanwori. Macdonald wants to use an extra, fifth defensive back on the field, to move Pro Bowl cornerback Devon Witherspoon from starting outside to inside at nickel in passing situations.

If Emmanwori can't be in the middle of the defense affecting New England in multiple ways including blitzing, the coach wants Witherspoon to be there.

Jones said the challenge of coming up with new schemes is invigorating Macdonald, on the eve of the defensive innovator's third season as a head coach.

"You can tell he's excited. He's dialin' stuff up, coming up with all kinds of things," Jones said.

There are questions with each of Macdonald's alternatives to go into nickel defense with a fifth defensive back if Emmanwori can't play.

Does he want to go to a third safety, beyond starters Julian Love and Ty Okada?

More to the point: Does he have even two healthy safeties?

Okada didn't practice Sunday. He has a newly reported hamstring issue.

So two of the three safeties on the 53-man, active roster are iffy to play Wednesday.

On the practice squad, the options for call-up include former Indianapolis Colts starter Rodney Thomas, second-year veteran Maxen Hook, 2025 contributor D'Anthony Bell and AJ Finley.

The coaches like Thomas' athleticism in the open field. He is back after missing time last month following hand surgery.

Bud Clark would have been the obvious candidate. But the rookie second-round draft choice broke his ankle in the second preseason game last month. He is out for the season.

Is Trevon Diggs, the former Dallas Cowboys All-Pro cornerback who signed in late August and practiced with the Seahawks for the first time the final week and a half of the preseason, going to be ready to play as the third cornerback when Macdonald wants to play nickel defense against New England? Diggs is on the practice squad trying to ramp up into playing shape and mastering the Seahawks defense after not practicing since January with Green Bay.

Defensive coordinator Aden Durde said following practice Sunday Diggs is good to go knowing enough of the defense to play

Is Avery Smith ready? The Seahawks traded with the Los Angeles Chargers for the undrafted rookie cornerback only one week ago. He had a great preseason for a Chargers defense similar in scheme to Seattle's.

Yet the rookie from Toledo knowing Macdonald's intricate defense enough to play outside cornerback after a week and a half with a new team is a tall ask.

Can they trust Nehemiah Pritchett? The unproven, third-year veteran began training camp as the third cornerback with Witherspoon playing inside. But Seattle's fifth-round draft choice in 2024 struggled with tackling. Veteran Noah Igbinoghene began taking some of Pritchett's reps with the starting defense in the middle of training camp last month.

The coaches weren't satisfied with Igbinoghene, either. The Seahawks cut him after they signed Diggs and signed Terrion Arnold , the former Detroit Lions first-round pick.

Arnold is now on the NFL commissioner's exempt list and unable to play as he faces eight felony charges in Florida.

Macdonald and the Seahawks could bypass their issue at third cornerback by welcoming back Tyrice Knight. It would reward Knight, a starting linebacker as a rookie in 2024 for Macdonald, for his standout training camp and preseason.

Seattle could use the three off-ball linebacker sets the defense worked in training camp. Knight and Drake Thomas, who beat out Knight as the starting weakside, "Will" inside linebacker last season, flank Jones in that alignment.

It's one more off-ball linebacker than the Seahawks played with, with Jones and Thomas, while in nickel and dime (five and six defensive backs) the majority of last season.

Three linebackers can an Emmanwori hedge until he is back full go.

Knight says the three-linebacker sets he's been working with Thomas and Jones aren't all that new to him.

"I mean, there's really no difference to me," Knight told The News Tribune before practice Sunday.

The fourth-round pick in 2024 said the role is like playing the Will linebacker in dime, six defensive-back sets, but that now he has more responsibilities to the wider side of the field in pass coverage.

Jones, the defense's signal-caller, loves the three-linebackers across the middle of the defense.

"Yeah, I think anytime we can add something, especially for defensive players (that) keep offenses off balance, that's really good," Jones said. "But I'm excited to see T-Knight come out there and ball with us.

"We love having three linebackers on the field. It's a little selfish thing with us linebackers.

"But he's been making plays throughout camp," Jones said of Knight. "He's deserved the opportunity to get out there with us. So I'm excited for it."

articles.title: Chivas and a show of class in San Luis Potosí
articles.summary: Guadalajara defeated Atlético de San Luis 0-3 on Matchday 7 of the 2026 Apertura, in a display of ruthlessness, pressure, and adaptability that once again hi...
articles.body:
Guadalajara defeated Atlético de San Luis 0-3 on Matchday 7 of the 2026 Apertura, in a display of ruthlessness, pressure, and adaptability that once again highlighted the wealth of resources in Gabriel Milito's team. Some matches are won by a single detail. Others, by an individual moment of brilliance. And then there are performances like Chivas' in San Luis, where the result ends up being merely a reflection of a dominance built through different phases of play.

The 0-3 win at Estadio Alfonso Lastras was a snapshot of what Guadalajara can offer when its pieces correctly execute the game plan. High pressure, clean buildup from the back, the ability to pin the opposing defensive line, and above all, excellent reading from the bench to change the course of the match when Atlético de San Luis tried to respond.

One of Guadalajara's main strengths was its pressing. Chivas constantly disrupted San Luis' buildup and, from that work, recovered the ball in areas that allowed them to attack with an advantage. The defensive structure also had an important adjustment with the return of Daniel Aguirre, who settled in as the right-sided stopper and gave the team a cleaner way out from the back.

Hugo Camberos and Roberto Alvarado did not have to cover great distances as wing-backs. Both played much higher up, more like wingers, which allowed Chivas to have greater presence and width in the opposing half. And when the match began to get bogged down, another virtue emerged: the ability to change roles without having to completely alter the structure.

Alvarado began to get involved much deeper in the buildup, moving closer to the first passes and helping give continuity to possessions. 'Piojo' not only contributed in the attacking half; he also became an important piece in playing out from the back.

Three forwards against three center-backsThe first goal perfectly summed up one of the ideas Gabriel Milito had laid out for the match: creating a three-versus-three scenario against Atlético de San Luis' center-backs. Ángel Sepúlveda, Ricardo Marín, and Santiago Sandoval were tasked with pinning back San Luis' defensive line. Sandoval, who essentially acted as a third striker, perfectly read the space that opened up between the center-backs and appeared there to finish and make it 0-1. It was not an isolated play. It was the consequence of an idea.

Chivas managed to give the home defenders clear references against the red-and-white attackers and, at the same time, found spaces to attack between the lines. The second goal once again showed that same intention.

Sepúlveda received the ball with his marker practically glued to him, but he used his body to shield it and laid it off first-time for Ricardo Marín. The Chivas striker took advantage of the move and finished brilliantly to extend the lead. Two goals, two examples of how Guadalajara managed to make the most of its attackers' qualities.

Milito moved the pieces againAtlético de San Luis changed its approach in the second half. The home side came out more aggressively, took possession, and for several minutes managed to push the match into Chivas' half. Chivas lost some control and the scenario seemed different from the first half. That was when another of Guadalajara's great strengths appeared: its ability to adjust.

Gabriel Milito changed two pieces and once again found the match. The introduction of Efraín Álvarez gave the team a player capable of staying wide on the left, but also of drifting inside. Kevin Castañeda came on to add presence between the lines and behind San Luis' midfielders, while Chivas sacrificed a striker to gain an extra man in that area.

The effect was immediate. Guadalajara once again found better connections and regained control of the ball. Even the first passes began to come from players we usually think of as attackers. Alvarado and Álvarez got involved from deeper positions, offering passing lanes and helping build attacks from the back.

That detail is important: Chivas did not rely solely on its center-backs or midfielders to start plays. Its own attackers were able to become builders.

The third, another display of combination playThe 0-3 scoreline put the finishing touch on the performance. Ricardo Marín once again played with his back to goal, pinned his marker, and laid the ball off precisely for Richard Ledezma, who faced the goal and unleashed a powerful shot that beat the San Luis goalkeeper.

A combination that once again put on display one of this Guadalajara side's great characteristics: the ability to create advantages through short combinations, movement, and players capable of interpreting different roles.

Ledezma also delivered very good minutes after coming on down the right wing. His contribution brought freshness and depth in the closing stages.

A team with answersThe win in San Luis matters because of the three points, but also because of everything it explains. Chivas was able to press, build, pin defenders back, attack spaces, adjust its height, and respond when the opponent changed its approach. It was a team that found solutions from its initial structure, but also from the bench. And that speaks to the number of resources Gabriel Milito has at his disposal.

Guadalajara showed that it can dominate a match in different ways. It can do so with high pressure, with positional attacks, with direct play into its forwards, or by creating superiority between the lines. On a difficult ground, the Rebaño delivered a complete performance and earned a convincing 0-3 win that allowed it to climb the standings. Chivas has resources. Milito has alternatives. And San Luis was further proof of that.

articles.title: Chicago White Sox aim to ‘get guys in the best spots’ with rotation tweaks heading into the stretch
articles.summary: Sunday served as another sign of the progress the Chicago White Sox have made this season. Their series finale against the Minnesota Twins at Rate Field was...
articles.body:
Sunday served as another sign of the progress the Chicago White Sox have made this season.

Their series finale against the Minnesota Twins at Rate Field was originally scheduled to start at 1:10 p.m. But it was flexed to a Sunday evening slot following a late July announcement to showcase the club in front of a national television audience.

"It's really cool," manager Will Venable said before the game. "People want to watch us play, and for good reason. The way these guys go out and handle their business, we have a bunch of young, exciting players and guys that are playing well and doing their jobs well, and doing it with definitely a distinct attitude.

The Sox made some adjustments to their pitching rotation in the days leading up to the contest, pushing Sean Burke's start from Sunday to Tuesday. They went with Bryan Hudson as an opener against the Twins as part of a bullpen game.

Venable said on Saturday that a "few different things" factored into the rotation tweaks.

"Just the off day (on Monday), have a chance to line some things up," Venable said. "And as we're looking ahead, trying to get guys in the best spots, there's some implications with rest, there's some implications with matchups.

"So just on the whole, as we evaluate all those things and have the off day to kind of change some things up, we went ahead and did it."

Burke and Davis Martin are scheduled to pitch Tuesday and Wednesday against the Pittsburgh Pirates at Rate Field. The starter for Thursday's series finale is to be announced.

Asked on Saturday if the Sept. 14-16 series at Cleveland was part of the decision, Venable said, "You could look at a lot of different things. That's way down the road. We've got a lot going on before that. It's really what it means mostly up front here to rest some guys."

The Sox have a two-game lead over the Guardians in the American League Central entering Sunday evening. The Guardians defeated the Detroit Tigers 3-2 in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon, their third walk-off win of the series.

After Sunday, the Sox will have 19 games remaining in the regular season. How the starting pitching performs will play a pivotal role in which team finishes first in the division.

"We are welcoming starters going out there and going deeper in games because it does reset the bullpen, but if that's not the case, then we'll continue to stay creative and find guys who cover innings and give us quality innings in the bullpen as well," general manager Chris Getz said on Friday.

Luis Castillo is among those starters working on adjustments. The right-hander has a 7.52 ERA in six starts since being acquired in a trade with the Seattle Mariners on Aug. 1 .

"I do think that when players come over in trades, it's a transition," Getz said. "Sometimes, players carry a little too much and carry the burden of trying to justify a trade and winning teammates over, and a manager over and coaches over, fans and media. That's just part of the transition. There's probably a little bit of that. Now, just mechanically, he did make some strides ( Thursday against the Houston Astros ). He did. There were some lower-half mechanics they were working on and that seemed to be in a much better place. The upper half, the shoulders, seem to be flying open a little bit more than it had in the past. I think the pitch shapes were trending in the right direction. The velocity was affected a little bit.

"He's not exactly where we want him to be or showing what he's capable of doing, but that doesn't mean we don't continue to work. That's kind of the beauty of what we do and what we've done. We'll continue to do so, find ways to solve for problems and issues and make adjustments. Davis Martin and Sean Burke are great examples of that. We hope to be able to apply that for Castillo and get him back on track."

Sox place outfielder Tommy Pham on the IL

The Sox placed recently acquired outfielder Tommy Pham on the 10-day injured list with a left calf strain. The move is retroactive to Thursday.

The Sox acquired Pham in a trade with the Philadelphia Phillies on Aug. 31. He has appeared in one game, going 0-for-1.

Venable said the injury occurred during defensive work on Saturday.

"He was working out on the field, felt something on his calf that grabbed on him," Venable said. "Was significant enough that we had to put him on the IL."

In the corresponding move, the Sox recalled catcher Edgar Quero from Triple-A Charlotte.

"As you look at Tommy, his role was really right-handed bat against lefties and in certain spots," Venable said. "And as we evaluated the options, felt very confident that Quero is the next best guy to fill that void."

articles.title: Enjoying the moment: Alcaraz steps it up to reach US Open quarter-finals
articles.summary: Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz, gaining confidence with every match, cruised into the US Open quarter-finals on Sunday with a comprehensive victory over T...
articles.body:
Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz, gaining confidence with every match, cruised into the US Open quarter-finals on Sunday with a comprehensive victory over Tommy Paul.

The second-seeded Spaniard, playing his first tournament after a four-month absence with a right wrist injury, beat Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 to reach his fifth quarter-final at Flushing Meadows -- where he won the first of his seven Grand Slam titles back in 2022.

"Really happy to see where my level is right now," Alcaraz said. "Beating Tommy Paul is always great feedback to see where you are, and (I'm) just really happy about everything I've done today.

"I think I returned pretty well. I saw really well the game today, what I had to do in every moment, using the right things in every moment. So I'm just really happy."

The 23-year-old, who claimed his seventh Grand Slam title at the Australian Open in January, had admitted to some trepidation as he opted to make his injury return at the final Grand Slam of the year.

After wins over Roman Safiullin, Jaime Faria and Wu Yibing, Alcaraz pointed to some rust -- a few more forehand errors than he liked to see and some suspect decision making on court.

But he put it all together against Paul, his first top-25 opponent of the tournament.

Alcaraz has now won seven of nine meetings with the American, and he dominated on Sunday, firing 33 winners from all points of the compass as he moved fluidly around the court, adjusting his return position to keep Paul off-balance.

Alcaraz finally gained the first break of the contest in the final game of a tight first set.

From there, it was almost all Alcaraz. He broke Paul twice in the second set and again early in the third.

He finished it off in style as he saved a pair of break points in the final game, the second with a swinging forehand volley followed by a forehand winner to set up the only match point he needed.

Paul certainly didn't see many weaknesses in the Spaniard's game.

"He's still hitting his forehand hard and off the court," Paul said. "I feel like he's maybe mixing things up on the return a little bit more.

"I think going into the match I saw his first-serve speed maybe was dropped a little bit from before he took time off, but I thought he made up with it with his first ball after his serve."

"I just had to be hard with myself, saying again the serves can be better," he said. "But I'm just happy, and I'm going to enjoy this moment, for sure."

articles.title: Iowa State goes 2-0 at Gaucho Invitational
articles.summary: SANTA BARBARA, Calif. – The Iowa State volleyball team put on a resilient display during its road trip to the West Coast, fighting through back-to-back four-...
articles.body:
SANTA BARBARA, Calif. – The Iowa State volleyball team put on a resilient display during its road trip to the West Coast, fighting through back-to-back four-set battles at the Thunderdome to improve to 4-1 on the season.

The Cyclones opened the invitational with a dramatic comeback victory over tournament host UC Santa Barbara on Thursday before outlasting Utah State in a Friday night thriller.

The Cyclones kicked off the action on Thursday by silencing a hostile crowd, bouncing back from an opening-set loss to secure an 18-25, 26-24, 25-20, 25-21 victory over UC Santa Barbara.

Iowa State's offense was highly efficient against the Gauchos, hitting a blistering .320 as a team. Sophomore outside hitter Nayeli Gonzalez paced the attack with a match-high 18 kills, while junior Nayeli Ti'a was right behind her with 17 kills and nine digs. Junior opposite Lilly Wachholz was incredibly efficient, posting 12 kills with only two errors on 19 swings for a spectacular .526 hitting percentage.

Setter Ava Martin directed the offense beautifully with 42 assists, and freshman libero Rachel Van Gorp anchored the defense with 13 digs. Despite UCSB's Sophia Wendlick and Gabi Martinez each registering 14 kills for the Gauchos, Iowa State's late-set execution made the difference.

Iowa State carried that momentum into Friday night, overcoming a fierce defensive challenge from Utah State to grind out a 25-20, 17-25, 28-26, 25-23 victory.

Wachholz was once again a major focal point for the Cyclones, hammering down a team-high 18 kills while hitting an efficient .484. Ti'a contributed a double-double with 11 kills and 12 digs, and middle blocker Daaliyah Kemp provided a huge offensive spark, converting six kills on a stellar .667 hitting percentage. Martin matched her Thursday performance with another 42 assists, while Van Gorp led the floor defense with 16 digs.

Utah State (0-4) proved to be a stubborn opponent, out-hitting the Cyclones .210 to .191. The Aggies were led by Sami Blackett's match-high 19 kills and 12 digs, alongside 11 kills from Olivia Ruy.

The match ultimately turned on high-pressure moments late in the sets. A grueling third set featured 11 tie scores and only a single lead change before Iowa State pulled away, 28-26. The fourth set was equally tight, featuring 10 ties and five lead changes before the Cyclones clinched the match, 25-23, to sweep their trip to the Thunderdome.

Iowa State hosts Iowa at Hilton Coliseum for the Iowa Corn Cy-Hawk Series Tuesday at 6:30 p.m.

articles.title: Howie Roseman reveals the one thing that will define Jalen Hurts in Philadelphia
articles.summary: Jalen Hurts enters a pivotal 2026 season with questions surrounding Philadelphia’s offense and his long-term future, but Eagles GM Howie Roseman just made hi...
articles.body:
Questions surrounding Jalen Hurts' long-term future in Philadelphia may be growing outside the organization, but Eagles general manager Howie Roseman isn't treating the 2026 season as an ultimatum for his quarterback.

Roseman pushed back against the idea that Hurts must prove himself this season to remain Philadelphia's starter, pointing instead to what the quarterback has accomplished since taking control of the offense.

For Roseman, winning remains the most important measurement.

"The barometer is winning football games," Roseman said during an appearance on 94 WIP.

Hurts has certainly done plenty of that.

Since entering the NFL in 2020, Hurts has compiled a 57-25 regular-season record as Philadelphia's starting quarterback. He has also taken the Eagles to two Super Bowls and helped deliver a championship during the 2024 season, earning Super Bowl MVP honors in the process.

Still, Philadelphia enters 2026 looking for significant improvement offensively.

The Eagles ranked just 23rd in passing yards last season at 194.3 per game and finished 19th in Total QBR. Despite having the NFL's highest-paid offense, Philadelphia ranked 19th in scoring at 22.3 points per game and struggled with three-and-outs.

Those shortcomings have resulted in major changes.

New offensive coordinator Sean Mannion has installed a West Coast-style system featuring concepts influenced by Sean McVay, Kyle Shanahan and Matt LaFleur.

One of the biggest developments has reportedly been Hurts' willingness to embrace those adjustments.

Left tackle Jordan Mailata has described Hurts as "all-in" on the new offense, while others inside the organization have praised his approach throughout the offseason.

Hurts signed a five-year, $255 million extension in 2023 that runs through 2028, although 2026 represents the final season in which his salary is fully guaranteed.

That contract situation will naturally create speculation.

Roseman, however, appears far more interested in Hurts' résumé than outside noise.

For Philadelphia, the mission remains simple: win.

And until Hurts stops doing that, Roseman sees little reason to question who should be leading the Eagles.

articles.title: What's at stake when the Chicago Cubs face the Brewers this week?
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs are in town to face Milwaukee for three games; just how crucial are those games in the playoff picture?
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers didn't exactly cloak themselves in glory during a 3-4 stretch against the Chicago Cubs and Cincinnati Reds last week, but with the same teams heading into American Family Field (starting Sept. 7), the Brewers' eight-game lead in the Central heading into last week has only been trimmed to seven.

The Brewers only really need to stave off a sweep at the hands of the Cubs to still feel comfortable with their division lead heading into the weekend; even one win should keep things relatively calm. The Brewers could easily clinch a playoff spot on the homestand, although it won't be the first two days against the Cubs.

The division will probably have to wait until the Brewers' final road trip.

Here's what to know about the three-game series against Chicago that begins on Labor Day.

Who's pitching in the series between the Brewers and Cubs?

All three games will air on Brewers.TV and AM-620 WTMJ radio. The game will also air on FOX on Tuesday.

Sept. 7, 1:10 p.m.: Milwaukee LHP Robert Gasser (4-5, 4.57) vs. Chicago LHP Matthew Boyd (8-3, 4.05).

Sept. 8, 6:40 p.m.: Milwaukee RHP Jacob Misiorowski (14-5, 1.97) vs. Chicago LHP David Peterson (7-8, 5.39).

Sept. 8, 6:40 p.m.: Milwaukee RHP Logan Henderson (9-3, 2.48) vs. Chicago RHP Kevin Gausman (9-11, 4.38).

Didn't the Brewers just see these three Cubs pitchers?

They sure did. A lot will feel the same this week with the Cubs and Reds back on the calendar for six games at American Family Field after the Brewers played on the road against those teams this past week. The Brewers won't see Clay Holmes, who held them in check during a 17-3 shellacking, but did do enough against Boyd and Peterson to secure wins (with a little help from the Cubs bullpen).

Henderson and Gausman will rematch after Gausman and his split-finger fastball flummoxed the Brewers in a 2-1 loss Thursday. The Brewers got to Boyd for three runs in 5⅓ innings and tagged Peterson for six in 3⅔.

Can the Brewers clinch a playoff spot during the series?

Yes, but it requires a lot to go right. The Brewers magic number to secure a playoff spot is seven, with the Diamondbacks and Padres straddling the final wild-card spot in the National League with 68 losses each. Those two have a three-game series against each other still on the schedule later in September, so we know one of them will get at least two more losses. That means the magic number is really five right now (since the Brewers have to only finish ahead of one of them to lock up a playoff spot).

The Brewers have the tiebreaker over the Diamondbacks and do not against the Padres, so the head-to-head number for the Brewers to officially finish better than Arizona is 6 and San Diego is 7.

Easiest path? Brewers sweep the Cubs, knocking three off the magic number and the Diamondbacks lose all three games at Kansas City, knocking the other three off. The best Arizona can do after that scenario is tie the Brewers at the end of the year, and the Brewers would have the tiebreaker.

Another scenario would involve the Brewers winning all three games and both San Diego and Arizona losing two of three (the Padres face Washington). Then, the Brewers would be in because their magic number to "eliminate" either one of them would be two, and the Brewers know one of them is guaranteed to lose twice more, so it's a done deal even if they don't know which team is the one "eliminated."

The last scenario would be Arizona and San Diego both getting swept and the Brewers winning two of three. We're in the same place as above, where the magic number is two but one of them is getting two more losses eventually to account for the final slashes off the magic number.

How early can the Brewers win the division?

A sweep against the Cubs would really help and account for half of the remaining 12 on the magic number tally. The Brewers would still be able to secure the Central by the end of the homestand on Sunday, but it requires nearly everything to go right. It's far more likely it happens on the upcoming three-city road trip to Pittsburgh, Baltimore and Philadelphia.

What do the Brewers need to do to get the tiebreaker over the Cubs?

Milwaukee needs to win just one game to lock up the season series and hold the tiebreaker. Thus, while the magic number is 12 heading into the week, a win Monday would actually slice that down to 9, since the goal is no longer to finish with an outright better record; a tie will do. The Brewers are 6-4 against the Cubs this year and need to get to seven wins in the 13-game season series.

The Cubs just won a series in Miami after splitting four games against the Brewers at Wrigley Field, but the Cubs had lost four of five series prior to that, and the one win over the White Sox required two walk-off victories. The Brewers have been scuffling a bit in the past few weeks, but they're still 12-8 over their last 20 games, while the Cubs are 9-11.

Pete Crow-Armstrong has been a behemoth against everyone else but quiet against Milwaukee

With his 40th home run on Sept. 6, outfielder Pete Crow-Armstrong is one step closer to winning the National League MVP award, especially with Shohei Ohtani ailing and seemingly unlikely to pitch the rest of the way. The defensive wizard center fielder PCA has a .946 OPS this year, with 33 stolen bases and 96 RBIs.

The funny thing is, Brewers fans haven't seen the best of PCA. Though he did hit a tough Logan Henderson pitch out to center field to account for Chicago's runs in a 2-1 win Thursday, it's his only extra-base hit against the Brewers this year in 10 games. He's batting 4 for 37 (.108) this season against Milwaukee. In his career, it's a .164 batting average and .620 OPS.

Either the Brewers know the best way to attack Crow-Armstrong or he's due.

Much has been made about how bad the Chicago Cubs bullpen has been lately, and it hasn't been dazzling. The Cubs have a 5.16 ERA since Aug. 20, though five teams in MLB have been worse, and Cincinnati, the other team in Milwaukee's recent orbit, has a 5.12 ERA. In the small sample since September started, the Cubs aren't even in the bottom third in bullpen ERA.

For the year, Chicago's 3.98 ERA is 12th best in baseball. You know who has been good out of the Cubs bullpen in longer relief? Aaron Civale.

articles.title: Houston Astros claim outfielder Jorge Barrosa off waivers from Arizona Diamondbacks
articles.summary: The Astros have started 11 different left fielders this year as they welcome another new outfielder in Jorge Barrosa.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros added a new outfielder to their evolving mix there Sunday, claiming Jorge Barrosa off waivers from the Arizona Diamondbacks .

Barrosa, 25, is a switch-hitter with poor offensive numbers and solid defensive metrics in limited time in the majors. He posted a .180/.241/.302 slash line and a 50 OPS-plus in 254 plate appearances across the past three seasons with the Diamondbacks, who designated him for assignment on Friday.

Barrosa has played all three outfield positions in the majors, mostly in center field, where he has accrued three defensive runs saved in 248 ⅔ innings this year, per Sports Info Solutions. The Astros said Barrosa will join them for their upcoming series in Philadelphia .

Houston optioned Jake Meyers to Triple-A Sugar Land to create an active roster spot for Barrosa. Pitcher Mike Burrows was transferred to the 60-day injured list to open a 40-man roster spot. Burrows has been on the IL retroactive to July 7, so this move does not impact timing of a potential return.

The Astros have started 11 different players in left field this year. Nelson Velázquez , claimed off waivers last month as a right-handed outfield bat, remains on the roster. They have also started eight different players in center field, including Daulton Varsho , their lone trade deadline acquisition.

Barrosa is out of minor-league options, meaning the Astros will need to keep him on the active roster or expose him to waivers. In their outfield group, none of Velázquez, Taylor Trammell , LaMonte Wade Jr. or Varsho can be optioned to the minors, either.

articles.title: Tiafoe and Michelsen win at the US Open as American men make a run at ending a Grand Slam drought
articles.summary: Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen are headed to the U.S. Open quarterfinals.  Ben Shelton had a chance to join them with a victory Sunday night.  The America...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen are headed to the U.S. Open quarterfinals. Ben Shelton had a chance to join them with a victory Sunday night.

The American men are making a real run at ending their lengthy Grand Slam drought.

The U.S. hasn't had a men's major champion since Andy Roddick won in Flushing Meadows in 2003, and there haven't even been many great opportunities in the more than two decades since.

But backed by the home crowd and in good form, the Americans had five players in the final 16 of a major for the first time since 1995 and will be a real threat in the second week of the final Grand Slam tournament of the season.

"We play so much outside of the States obviously, a lot of time in Europe," Tiafoe said. "This sport's so international, so to be able to play in front of friends, family, loved ones, is amazing. They don't get to see you much, so you want to put on a show."

The No. 11 seed beat 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (1), 6-4, 7-6 (6) to move within a victory of his third appearance in the U.S. Open semifinals. To get there he'll have to beat Michelsen, who has been the dominant player in this year's tournament.

The 22-year-old from California beat No. 27 Tomas Etcheverry 7-6 (6), 6-4, 6-4 and is the only man who has yet to drop a set in the tournament.

"We've been working really hard to get to this point and I'm really happy but not super surprised because of all the work I put in my whole life," Michelsen said after reaching his first Grand Slam quarterfinal.

The winner of his match against Tiafoe will face No. 2-seeded Carlos Alcaraz or the winner of the fourth-round match between No. 8 Shelton and Stefanos Tsitsipas in the semifinals.

All four men's matches Sunday had a U.S. player in it, and the Americans grabbed two of the first three. Only Alcaraz, the defending champion, was able to turn back a player from the host country, beating No. 20 seed Tommy Paul in the afternoon.

The Americans still had a chance to get one more quarterfinalist Monday when No. 14 seed Learner Tien faces Karen Khachanov.

The closest the Americans came to ending the drought was two years ago at the U.S. Open, when Taylor Fritz beat Tiafoe in the first all-American Grand Slam semifinal since 2005 to become the first American man in a major final since Roddick in 2009. Jannik Sinner beat Fritz in straight sets for the title.

The Americans had eight players in the round of 16 in the 1995 U.S. Open, advancing three to the semifinals. Pete Sampras beat Jim Courier in the semis and then No. 1 Andre Agassi in the final.

The U.S. expected to have multiple men's title contenders in that era, but some of the men have grown tired now of the annual discussion of the drought. Meanwhile, Coco Gauff has collected two trophies in recent years and Jessica Pegula has reached No. 3 in the world.

"There have been a really consistent chunk of players, Jess, Coco, you know, have been at the top and inside the top five for the last I don't know how many years," Taylor Townsend said after losing to women's No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka on Sunday. "Ben, Frances, Tommy, Taylor, it's just such a great group of men as well."

articles.title: NBC breaks silence on Michigan vs. WMU clock controversy with televised statement
articles.summary: NBC has finally addressed Saturday night's controversial clock management during Michigan versus Western Michigan.
articles.body:
It's unlikely that talk of Saturday night's explosively controversial final moments during Michigan versus Western Michigan will die down anytime soon. Nearly 24 hours later, however, NBC has finally offered an official statement on the controversial moment .

In the final seconds of Saturday night's tilt between Michigan and Western Michigan, quarterback Bryce Underwood's Hail Mary heave fell incomplete as the Wolverines looked to avoid a devastating upset in their first game of the season. While it looked as if Western Michigan was set to complete the upset, as the clock hit zero before the ball hit a player on the failed try, the referees ended up adding a second to the clock to allow Michigan one last attempt. Underwood ended up connecting with JJ Buchanan on the final Hail Mary try as Michigan walked off their opponents 13-12.

According to a statement and footage from the Big Ten released on Sunday, "Western Michigan's #18 started his jump from an established out-of-bounds position (left foot) and made contact with the ball with one second remaining on the clock". That footage contradicts what the stadium's clock and NBC's broadcast clock stated as the play ended, causing immense confusion amongst college football fans as the dust continues to settle on this controversial moment.

Then later on Sunday, NBC released its own statement via broadcaster John Fanta during halftime of Washington vs. Washington State.

The official time of the game is kept by the Big Ten. Our cameras are not the official arbiter of timekeeping within the game. That is the Big Ten and game officials' responsibility. After the game last night, the Big Ten released a statement and raw video from its replay process that showed how and why the decision was made. Here's a look back at that video, and with the ball hitting the defensive back for Western Michigan, that gave Michigan another second and one last play where JJ Buchanan came up big.

NBC immediately cut to commercial after the statement.

While it's good to have an official statement from NBC, it's hard to see this controversy dying down anytime soon given the discrepancy between what fans saw in the stadium and on TV and what the referees saw in their replay.

articles.title: Rams star says NFL teams ‘hate us’ after Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald additions spark ‘new Dodgers’ comparison
articles.summary: The Rams know exactly how the rest of the NFL feels about them. They are being called the new Dodgers, and they are fine with it.
articles.body:
The Rams know exactly how the rest of the NFL feels about them. They are being called the new Dodgers, and they are fine with it.

Quentin Lake has expanded on the comparison after Los Angeles stacked their defence this off-season.

"You know all these other teams probably hate us," the Rams safety said, per the Los Angeles Times' Gary Klein. "They think we're like the new Dodgers or something like that."

Lake owns the 'new Dodgers' label as Garrett and Donald promise big

The Dodgers have won back-to-back World Series, so the comparison says plenty about the hype in Los Angeles.

The Rams landed reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett in the biggest trade of the off-season, then watched Aaron Donald return from two years of retirement days later.

Opponents are not thrilled. One NFL GM told insider Jordan Schultz that Donald signing with Los Angeles "is so f*****."

The cost was steep. The Rams sent 2024 first-round pick and Defensive Rookie of the Year Jared Verse to Cleveland, along with a bevy of draft picks including their 2027 first-rounder.

Garrett set the single-season sack record last year and signed a four-year, $160 million pact in LA, with $123.6 million guaranteed.

The early signs are good on the injury front too. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Garrett had a knee issue in camp but is ramping up.

"He's been ramping up slowly, but surely. Been lifting a lot of weights. Now, he's on the practice field, so I'm hearing he should be good as well," Fowler said.

Sean McVay confirmed on Sunday that Garrett will practice.

That is a scary prospect for offences. The Rams finished seventh in sacks last season and ranked fourth in pressure rate, even though their pass defence was only 19th in the league.

Adding Garrett to that front, and Donald to the middle of it, changes the maths completely.

There is one headache to sort. Over The Cap projects the Rams $1.3 million over the cap once top-51 salaries count on September 9.

That is a small price for a super team. The hate from the rest of the league is part of the deal now, and the Rams are wearing it like a badge of honour.

articles.title: Patriots vs. Seahawks Sunday injury report: TreVeyon Henderson among 3 non-participants
articles.summary: The first injury report of the 2026 NFL season.
articles.body:
The New England Patriots continued preparations for the 2026 regular season down three.

Running back TreVeyon Henderson, center Ben Brown and defensive tackle Christian Barmore stayed sidelined during Sunday's practice as the Super Bowl LX rematch closes in.

Here's the first injury report ahead of Wednesday's 8:20 p.m. ET kickoff against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field.

Henderson has not practiced since hurting his right ankle on Aug. 24 . With the 2025 PFWA All-Rookie selection's Week 1 availability in doubt, fellow running backs Hassan Haskins and Lan Larison loom on New England's practice squad as elevation candidates. As for the non-participants in the Patriots' trenches, Brown's knee injury stems from the preseason opener , while Barmore marked a new absence on Labor Day weekend due to a knee ailment of his own.

No member of the 53-man roster in Foxborough practiced in a limited capacity on Sunday. But four went to that degree in Seattle, including Emmanwori at safety. Working back from ankle surgery saw him begin training camp on the physically unable to perform list, the No. 35 overall pick in last year's draft class amassed 81 tackles, 2.5 sacks, 11 passes defensed and one interception during his rookie campaign en route to a ring.

A trio of on-the-mend Seahawks were listed as full participants following Sunday's practice. But it'd be a clean slate in that department for the Patriots.

articles.title: Controversy deepens as Zamalek treasurer threatens to take Zizo contract discrepancy to Parliament
articles.summary: The dispute surrounding Ahmed Sayed “Zizo” has moved beyond the football authorities after Zamalek treasurer Hossam El-Mandouh revealed plans to raise questi...
articles.body:
The dispute surrounding Ahmed Sayed "Zizo" has moved beyond the football authorities after Zamalek treasurer Hossam El-Mandouh revealed plans to raise questions over player contracts in Parliament.

El-Mandouh, who is also a member of the Egyptian House of Representatives, believes the figures surrounding Zizo's contract warrant further scrutiny and has called for state intervention in reviewing footballers' agreements.

Hossam El-Mandouh plans to raise Zizo issue in Parliament

El-Mandouh's comments centre on an alleged difference between the amount a player requested from Zamalek and the value of the contract registered with the Egyptian Football Association.

"There was a player who asked us (Zamalek) for 80 million pounds per season, and then we hear that his contract at the Football Association is only 5 million pounds. So is this something logical?"

The Zamalek treasurer subsequently confirmed that Zizo was the player he was referring to, while claiming that the issue is not necessarily limited to the former Zamalek player.

"Of course I mean Zizo, and there are other contracts in the same form. I will raise this matter in Parliament, and the state must intervene to review the files of players' contracts. When Hany Abo Rida, president of the Egyptian Football Association, says that there are valid contracts and others that are not valid, this certainly raises question marks."

That could give the long-running dispute another dimension, with El-Mandouh now intending to bring his concerns before Parliament rather than keeping them within the confines of football's governing bodies.

Zizo's departure from Zamalek has already become a contentious issue after he declined to renew his contract before joining Al-Ahly on a free transfer. The two sides have subsequently lodged complaints with the Egyptian Football Association.

El-Mandouh's latest intervention puts the focus on the documentation and figures surrounding footballers' contracts, while his proposed parliamentary move could bring further attention to the dispute involving Zizo.
